ai.glance: Possibly the most reproduced image in art history, this woodblock print shows boats battling a rogue wave with Mount Fuji in the background. Originally sold for the price of two bowls of noodles, it influenced Van Gogh, Monet, and Debussy.

story.receipt: Hokusai at age 75: 'From the age of six I had a mania for drawing... At seventy-three I finally learned something about the true nature of things. When I am a hundred and ten, everything I draw, a dot or a line, will be alive.' The print sold for 20 mon-about the price of two bowls of noodle soup.
story.surface_layer: A massive wave crests in the foreground, its foam clawing like white fingers at the sky. Three oshiokuri-bune (fast cargo boats) full of fishermen navigate the trough, their passengers clinging low. In the distance, rendered impossibly small by the wave's scale, Mount Fuji sits serene beneath a clear sky, its snow-capped peak echoing the wave's white foam. The composition creates a visual rhyme: the great wave mirrors Fuji's cone, the foam echoes its snow.
story.type_aesthetic: Ukiyo-e woodblock print using revolutionary imported Prussian blue pigment alongside traditional organic indigo. Western-influenced single-point perspective (learned from Dutch prints at Nagasaki) combined with Japanese compositional asymmetry. Multiple wood blocks carved for different colors, printed in edition of approximately 5,000-8,000 impressions.
story.core_philosophy: The sublime contrast between human vulnerability and natural forces-and the persistence of the sacred amid chaos. Fuji represents permanence, the wave represents flux. The fishermen, nearly invisible, represent humanity caught between. Hokusai signed it 'Hokusai, the old man mad about painting.'
story.cultural_context: Created around 1831 when Hokusai was approximately 70 years old, as part of the series 'Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji' (actually 46 prints). Japan's Tokugawa shogunate enforced sakoku (closed country) policy, but Dutch trade at Nagasaki brought Prussian blue pigment (Berlin blue), enabling the deep blues that define this print. The series capitalized on a Fuji pilgrimage boom and a new middle-class tourism culture.

observation_details.label: The Wave's Claw
observation_details.value: The foam fingers reaching downward were a Hokusai innovation-they give the wave predatory menace and may have influenced European Art Nouveau

observation_details.label: Mount Fuji
observation_details.value: Tiny but stable at center, Fuji is both a compositional anchor and spiritual symbol-the eternal amid the transient

observation_details.label: The Boats
observation_details.value: Oshiokuri-bune were fast boats that delivered fresh fish to Edo. The crew (about 8 per boat) crouch low, showing practiced survival technique

observation_details.label: Prussian Blue
observation_details.value: Imported from Europe via Dutch traders, this synthetic pigment enabled the deep blues impossible with traditional plant-based indigo

work_relations.note: Monet was an avid collector of Japanese ukiyo-e prints. The flattened perspective, cropped compositions, and decorative patterning of works like Hokusai's influenced his approach to the water lily pond, encouraging views without a traditional horizon line.

Like many of his contemporaries, Monet was influenced by Japanese Ukiyo-e woodblock prints. The flattened perspective, unconventional composition, and focus on transient natural phenomena seen in prints by artists like Hokusai are reflected in this work.

Like many Impressionists, Monet was influenced by Japanese ukiyo-e prints. The asymmetrical compositions, cropped views, and flattened perspectives of artists like Hokusai offered a new visual language visible in the framing of this scene.

The series capitalized on a Fuji pilgrimage boom and a new middle-class tourism culture.
